overview: EROAD is a New Zealand-founded transport-technology company that sells in-vehicle telematics hardware bundled with a subscription SaaS platform for fleet management, regulatory compliance (New Zealand electronic Road User Charges, US Electronic Logging Device/IFTA tax reporting), safety and vehicle tracking. It operates through three regions -- New Zealand (its largest, most profitable and most defensible market as the incumbent electronic RUC provider), North America (a subscale, loss-making business now being deliberately right-sized after a major customer loss and a US$134.7m FY26 goodwill/intangible impairment against the 2021/22 Coretex acquisition), and a smaller but fast-growing Australia. The company is dual-listed on the NZX and ASX (ticker ERD on both) and reports in NZD with a 31 March fiscal year end.

business_model.summary: Revenue is a hardware-plus-subscription model: EROAD installs an in-cab telematics unit (largely rented/bundled rather than sold outright) and charges a recurring monthly SaaS subscription per contracted unit covering RUC/ELD compliance, fleet tracking, safety and fuel-tax reporting. FY26 subscription revenue was $185.9m of $195.2m total revenue (~95%), making the business predominantly recurring; the balance is transactional hardware and fee revenue. Management tracks Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR, $174.3m at FY26) and monthly ARPU (Average Revenue Per Unit, $60.88 group-wide at FY26) as the core KPIs, alongside Asset Retention Rate (contracted-unit retention) by region. Historically EROAD also disclosed Future Contracted Income (FCI), a multi-year backlog metric reflecting the length of customer contracts.
business_model.customer_type: B2B -- commercial trucking/freight fleets, waste and utility operators, government/transport agencies; ranges from small-to-medium fleets to large enterprise accounts (EROAD defines 'Enterprise' as >$100k ARR); NZ also has an emerging B2G/B2C dimension as universal electronic RUC could extend the model to light vehicles
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand $102.0m (52% of FY26 revenue, +1.1% YoY), North America $74.4m (38%, -7.1% YoY), Australia $18.8m (10%, +40.3% YoY); unit count 124,470 NZ / 87,830 North America / 26,089 Australia at FY26 year end

competitive_position.market_position: Dominant, first-mover incumbent in New Zealand electronic RUC (management states ~86% of heavy-vehicle and ~85% of light-vehicle eRUC by value processed through EROAD, and 56% of NZ heavy-vehicle RUC kilometres on its platform); a much smaller disrupter/challenger brand in the fragmented but growing Australian market; a subscale, declining-share player in the vastly larger and more competitive North American ELD/fleet-telematics market, where Samsara, Geotab, Motive and Verizon Connect are far larger, better-funded and increasingly commoditising the hardware layer

moat_factors.description: First and largest electronic RUC provider in New Zealand since 2009, with deep integration into NZTA/government processes, brand recognition among fleet operators, and a nationwide installer network -- durable but not immune to reform (see risks)
Hardware fitted in-cab plus multi-year contracts and compliance workflows create switching friction once a fleet is onboarded; NZ asset retention rate was 91.9% at FY26

Two decades of accumulated fleet, safety and RUC/ELD compliance data and process knowledge across three regulatory regimes; management frames this as a structural barrier versus 'software-only' rivals given the complexity of hardware, integrations and compliance
Strong brand recognition in NZ; positioned as a credible 'disrupter' challenger brand in Australia leveraging NZ success (Cleanaway enterprise win)

EROAD is subscale relative to Samsara, Geotab, Motive and Verizon Connect, who have far larger R&D budgets, broader platforms and more data; this contributed directly to the loss of its largest US customer (Old Dominion, ~$9m ARR) to a cheaper competitor amid tariff-driven cost pressure

weaknesses: North America (38% of group revenue) is structurally subscale against much larger, better-capitalised US competitors and has been in revenue/ARR/unit-count decline (ARR -19.8% and units -15.9% in FY26)
Group profitability has been repeatedly disrupted by one-off costs, accounting-estimate changes and a large impairment, making underlying earnings power hard to assess from reported GAAP figures
Heavy reliance on a single very large customer loss (Old Dominion, ~$9m ARR) materially moving group results shows customer concentration risk in North America

History of major capital-structure stress: the 2021/22 debt- and equity-funded Coretex acquisition led to integration problems, a CEO change, and ultimately a near-total write-off of the North American intangible/goodwill base

growth_drivers: New Zealand universal electronic RUC: the NZ Government confirmed in August 2025 its intention to replace fuel excise duty with distance-based electronic RUC for all ~4.7 million vehicles (including light passenger vehicles), with legislation targeted for passage in 2026 and the market opening to third-party providers from around 2027 -- EROAD frames this as a 'once-in-a-generation' expansion of its addressable market from the ~3% of vehicles (heavy/diesel) currently on RUC to the full national fleet; only around 3% of RUC transactions currently flow electronically outside heavy vehicles today per EROAD's own materials, implying a large greenfield opportunity if EROAD can capture meaningful share

Australia enterprise expansion: ARR +73% YoY to A$21.9m in FY26, underpinned by a 5-year Cleanaway agreement covering 3,000+ heavy vehicles (adding over A$5m ARR as it rolls out, ~24% deployed and on track for full implementation by November 2026) and a stated strategy to 'roll out the AU playbook' and expand sales presence
Disciplined North American repositioning toward free-cash-flow neutrality/breakeven rather than growth, which should stem the region's cash drain even without a return to growth

AI-driven operating leverage: management is investing in AI ('AI Native' strategic pillar) for internal workflow automation, platform modernisation and enhanced customer/data insights, aimed at improving margins without proportional headcount growth

New product initiatives in NZ RUC ecosystem: a direct-to-consumer app (targeted winter 2026), an SMB solution (targeted summer 2026), and OEM/third-party ecosystem partnerships (targeted mid-2027) to broaden reach ahead of/alongside universal eRUC rollout

Completion of the 4G hardware upgrade programme (73,000 units upgraded, ~88% renewal rate) removes a multi-year drag on reported free cash flow and should improve reported (not just normalised) FCF from FY27

business.description: Competing against far larger, better-funded rivals (Samsara, Geotab, Motive, Verizon Connect) with greater R&D budgets and data scale; EROAD lost its largest US customer (~$9m ARR, ~10,000+ units) to a competitor offering a cheaper solution amid tariff-driven freight-volume pressure, directly triggering the FY26 impairment and strategic reset

A single customer non-renewal (Old Dominion) was large enough to materially move group ARR, revenue and drive a $134.7m impairment -- North America's enterprise-weighted customer base leaves the region exposed to similar step-changes

The FY26 transformation (regional operating model, new executive team, five strategic priorities) is very recent (from October 2025) and unproven; management itself acknowledges 'an erosion of focus on our customers' drove the FY26 result, and multiple senior leadership changes (Executive Chair stepping into an executive capacity for up to nine months, co-CEO resignation, new CFO and regional GMs) create transition risk
North America asset retention rate fell to 80.1% at FY26 (from higher historically), well below NZ's 91.9% and Australia's 95.8%, evidencing accelerating churn in the weakest region

financial.risk: Balance sheet impairment and net working capital deficit
financial.description: FY26 goodwill/intangible impairment of $134.7m cut net assets from $331.7m to $172.3m and drove a $161.1m net loss; as at 31 March 2026 current liabilities exceeded current assets by $3.8m (a net working capital deficit), though the FY26 accounts are prepared on a going-concern basis and management notes this is not expected to result in a cash outflow

Bank facilities ($65m, syndicate of ANZ, BNZ and Kiwibank) extended to October 2027 with covenants including net leverage reducing to 1.00x by June 2026 and interest coverage ≥4.00x; total liquidity was only $49.0m (cash $10.1m plus facility headroom $38.9m) at FY26 year end -- modest headroom for a company still absorbing transformation costs

FY26 saw a $10.7m reclassification of R&D from capex to opex after introducing a minimum capitalisation threshold, plus a shortened useful economic life on intangibles (3-5 years from 5-10 years) -- both signal historically aggressive capitalisation that is now being unwound, and the pattern of frequent 'change in accounting estimate' items (accounting for $18.2m of FY26 EBIT impact) makes reported earnings volatile and comparability across periods difficult

Reports in NZD but North America (USD) and Australia (AUD) subsidiaries expose consolidated ARR/revenue to currency translation; FY26 ARR was reported as -0.5% in NZD but -1.4% in constant currency, showing FX partially flattered the headline number

regulatory.risk: NZ universal RUC collection model uncertainty
regulatory.description: The Government's move to universal electronic RUC is EROAD's single biggest opportunity but also a structural risk to its current incumbency: legislation is still being finalised (targeted 2026) and the eventual Code of Practice, provider-approval process and market structure are undecided; EROAD has publicly opposed NZTA acting as both regulator and retail eRUC provider, indicating the collection model could be opened to new entrants or centralised in ways that erode rather than extend EROAD's current dominant position (currently ~86% of heavy-vehicle and ~85% of light-vehicle eRUC by value)

Management directly attributed the loss of its largest US customer to Trump-administration tariffs compressing freight volumes (~10% reduction cited) and pushing customers toward cheaper telematics alternatives -- an ongoing macro/trade-policy risk to the North American customer base

regulatory.risk: Data privacy in a universal RUC rollout
regulatory.description: Extending distance-based road charging to millions of light/passenger vehicles raises privacy considerations that have already been flagged publicly by the NZ Privacy Commissioner, which could shape technical/consent requirements for any provider including EROAD

macro.description: North American revenue is directly linked to US trucking/freight volumes, which have been pressured by tariffs and a soft freight cycle; a prolonged downturn would continue to pressure the region EROAD is trying to stabilise

EROAD is a micro-cap (market capitalisation roughly NZ$100-150m at current depressed prices) with historically volatile, thinly-traded shares -- reported ~8%+ weekly price moves in recent periods -- making entry/exit and price discovery difficult for investors

Modest net borrowings mean direct interest-rate sensitivity is limited relative to larger leveraged infrastructure peers, but a weak balance sheet increases refinancing sensitivity to any rate or credit-market deterioration

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global fleet telematics/SaaS compliance is a structurally growing category (electrification, safety mandates, ELD/RUC compliance, fuel-efficiency and emissions tracking), but the North American segment has become intensely competitive and increasingly commoditised at the hardware layer, compressing pricing power for subscale players; New Zealand's shift to universal electronic RUC is a rare, largely non-discretionary, policy-driven expansion of the addressable market for RUC-specialist providers
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate -- revenue is subscription-based and relatively sticky, but new unit sales/installs and hardware revenue track freight and transport-sector activity, and North American revenue is exposed to US trucking-freight cyclicality and trade policy
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate -- modest absolute debt levels but tight liquidity headroom means funding costs and covenant compliance matter more than for a larger, better-capitalised peer
key_input_costs: In-vehicle hardware/semiconductor components (telematics units, now on 4G)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 annual results (year ended 31-Mar-2026): revenue $195.2m (+0.4%), ARR $174.3m (-0.5%), reported EBIT loss of $(155.9)m (Normalised EBIT $2.9m) driven by a $134.7m non-cash impairment of North American goodwill/intangibles plus $18.2m of accounting-estimate changes and $5.9m of one-off costs; net loss after tax $(161.1)m; normalised FCF $14.4m (FCF margin 7.4%, down from 12.1% in FY25); introduced initial FY27 guidance framework (low-single-digit NZ growth, double-digit AU growth, NA managed for cash discipline) without specific numeric targets

H1 FY2026 interim results (six months to 30-Sep-2025): revenue $99.1m (+3.3%), positive free cash flow of $6.2m, but a reported net loss of $144.2m driven by the same $134.7m North American goodwill/intangible impairment applied in October 2025; FY26 guidance reset to reflect the ANZ pivot and the large NA customer non-renewal: revenue $197-203m, ARR $175-183m, FCF margin 5-8% (normalised for the 4G upgrade programme)

Strategic reset: the Board applied the North American goodwill/intangible impairment, appointed John Scott as Executive Chair (for up to nine months in an executive capacity) to lead a business-wide reset, and Mark Heine became CEO while co-CEO David Kenneson (who had led the North American push) resigned effective 31-Oct-2025; company shifted from a global to a regional operating model and explicitly refocused strategy on New Zealand and Australia, with North America to be run for cash generation rather than growth

Loss of EROAD's largest North American customer, Old Dominion Freight Line (~$9m annual revenue, 10,000+ driver-monitoring units -- acquired via the 2021/22 Coretex acquisition), which switched to a lower-cost competitor; CEO Mark Heine attributed the loss in part to US tariffs reducing freight volumes (~10%) and pushing customers toward cheaper telematics alternatives

NZ Government confirmed its intention to replace fuel excise duty with a universal, distance-based electronic Road User Charges system covering all ~4.7 million NZ vehicles (including light/passenger vehicles), with legislation targeted for 2026 passage and the market opening to third-party providers from around 2027; EROAD publicly supports the shift and has proposed a low-cost ($40) smart-tag device for mass-market uptake while opposing NZTA acting as both regulator and retail provider

Australia's Cleanaway enterprise rollout (5-year agreement, 3,000+ heavy vehicles, A$5m+ ARR) progressing at ~20 installs/day, ~24% complete at FY26 year end, targeting full implementation by November 2026

Share price approximately NZ$0.985, down roughly 66% from the 52-week high of NZ$2.94, reflecting the compounding effect of the FY26 impairment/loss, the North American customer loss and strategic reset, reduced/uncertain guidance, and ongoing execution risk around the turnaround; the price has historically been highly volatile (reported ~8%+ average weekly moves) consistent with a thinly-traded micro-cap

items.notes: Framed as a 'stable, cash-generative base' with structural upside optionality from universal eRUC not yet quantified in guidance
Continuation of enterprise-led expansion (Cleanaway rollout) and operating leverage

items.target: Free cash flow discipline / repositioning, no explicit growth target
items.vs_prior: changed -- growth ambition abandoned in favour of cash discipline
items.notes: Region to be 'managed with a more focused operating model' to secure the existing revenue base rather than pursue growth; explicit qualitative target of FCF neutrality mentioned in the FY26 results presentation

items.target: Positive free cash flow across all regions
items.vs_prior: maintained emphasis, no specific numeric FY27 FCF margin given at FY26 results
items.notes: FY26 results presentation states the company 'remains focused on ... delivering positive free cash flow' but FY27 guidance introduced at the FY26 results was qualitative only (no revenue/ARR/FCF-margin numeric ranges disclosed for FY27 as of 25-May-2026)

guidance.management_commentary: Executive Chair John Scott described FY26 as reflecting 'the past' with the business intending to 'look different' going forward, citing an 'erosion of focus on our customers' as the core cause of the year's problems and outlining five strategic priorities (Operational Excellence, Product Excellence, Customer Intimacy, becoming AI Native, and 'Winning Universal eRUC'). Management explicitly reframed FY27 guidance around ANZ self-funding ('each region should be self-funding') with North America targeted for cash-flow neutrality rather than growth. The FY26 guidance given at the H1 FY26 results (November 2025) -- revenue $197-203m, ARR $175-183m, FCF margin 5-8% -- was reaffirmed at that time as 'unchanged' following the October 2025 reset, but the FY26 full-year actual result (revenue $195.2m, ARR $174.3m) came in modestly below the bottom of that reaffirmed range on revenue and at the low end on ARR, and FY26 FCF margin (7.4% normalised) landed within the guided range.

bull_case: New Zealand universal electronic RUC is a rare, policy-driven expansion of EROAD's core addressable market, potentially extending its RUC business from ~3.5m heavy/diesel vehicles today toward the full ~4.7m NZ vehicle fleet, leveraging an incumbency position (~85-86% of eRUC value processed) that a new entrant would need years to replicate

The FY26 impairment and reset draw a clear line under the failed North American growth strategy -- ANZ (NZ + Australia) alone generated $19.5m of normalised free cash flow in FY26, and management's new strategy of making North America merely cash-flow neutral, rather than continuing to fund its losses, should materially improve consolidated free cash flow if executed

Australia is EROAD's fastest-growing and highest-momentum segment (ARR +73% YoY), underpinned by a large, multi-year enterprise contract (Cleanaway) still mid-rollout, in a market EROAD frames as fragmented and winnable using its NZ playbook

The share price has fallen roughly 66% from its 52-week high and now trades at a small fraction of the company's 2021 capital-raise price (NZ$5.58/share) and well below Volaris/Constellation Software's historical (2023) all-cash takeover offer of NZ$1.30/share -- a sign the market may already be pricing in a very pessimistic turnaround outcome, leaving asymmetric upside if the ANZ-focused reset succeeds

Completion of the 4G hardware upgrade programme (88% renewal rate) removes a recurring multi-year cash drag, which should mechanically lift reported (not just normalised) free cash flow from FY27 onward even without further margin improvement
bear_case: The turnaround is very early-stage (initiated October 2025) and unproven -- management concedes the FY26 result reflects 'an erosion of focus on our customers,' multiple senior leadership changes are still bedding in, and FY27 guidance issued at the FY26 result was qualitative only, with no numeric revenue, ARR or FCF targets, signalling limited near-term visibility even from management itself

North America (still ~38% of group revenue) remains structurally subscale against Samsara, Geotab, Motive and Verizon Connect, evidenced by a rapidly deteriorating asset retention rate (80.1% at FY26, the weakest of the three regions) and a large customer loss driven partly by cheaper competitor offerings -- there is no guarantee 'cash-flow neutral' is achievable before further customer attrition erodes the base further

The NZ universal eRUC opportunity cuts both ways: the exact collection/provider model is still undecided (legislation only targeted for 2026 passage, market not open to competition until ~2027), and EROAD's own public opposition to NZTA acting as retail provider signals real uncertainty about whether the eventual regulatory design preserves or erodes its current incumbency advantage

Balance sheet capacity is thin -- a $(161.1)m FY26 net loss cut net assets from $331.7m to $172.3m, current liabilities exceeded current assets by $3.8m at year end, and total liquidity was only $49.0m against ongoing transformation costs, leaving limited room for further setbacks without additional capital or covenant stress

A history of accounting-estimate volatility (capitalisation-threshold changes, shortened intangible useful lives, recurring 'one-off' and 'normalised' adjustments) makes it difficult to trust reported figures at face value, and the pattern of repeated downward guidance resets (FY26 guidance reset once already in October 2025, prior years also saw goodwill impairments) raises the risk of further negative surprises as the ANZ-only strategy is executed
